clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive Leigh syndrome variant caused by LRPPRC mutations; a founder missense variant predominates in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec.
LRPPRC stabilises and polyadenylates mitochondrial messenger RNAs, so its loss causes a tissue-specific cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) deficiency that is most marked in brain and liver.
The chronic phenotype includes developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features and persistently elevated blood lactate.
The defining and life-threatening feature is recurrent acute metabolic crises with severe lactic acidosis and hepatic dysfunction, typically triggered by infection, fasting or other catabolic stress.
Crises carry high mortality and can progress rapidly to coma and death; most deaths occur during such episodes in early childhood.
Neuroimaging shows the classic Leigh pattern of bilateral symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem signal change.
Children may be relatively stable between crises, which can lead carers to underestimate the risk of decompensation.
Management is preventive and supportive, centred on avoidance of catabolism, prompt aggressive treatment of intercurrent illness, and crisis-anticipating sick-day planning.
reference.pathophysiology: LRPPRC encodes a leucine-rich pentatricopeptide-repeat protein that, together with SLIRP, binds mitochondrial messenger RNAs to maintain their stability, polyadenylation and coordinated translation. The founder variant destabilises the protein, lowering steady-state levels of several mtDNA-encoded transcripts and disproportionately impairing assembly of cytochrome c oxidase in brain and liver. The resulting failure of oxidative phosphorylation produces chronic lactic acidaemia and the subacute necrotising encephalopathy lesions characteristic of Leigh syndrome, while a low threshold for energy failure under catabolic stress precipitates the fulminant acidotic and hepatic crises. The abruptness and tissue selectivity of these crises reflect the tissue-specific dependence on LRPPRC-supported mitochondrial gene expression.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic causes of Leigh syndrome (mtDNA MT-ATP6, SURF1, nuclear complex I or IV assembly defects)
Biotinidase deficiency and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease
Organic acidaemias and urea-cycle disorders presenting with encephalopathic crises
Fatty-acid oxidation defects with hepatic decompensation
additionalInvestigations: Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate with the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
LRPPRC sequencing and targeted founder-variant testing
Respiratory-chain enzyme assays showing isolated complex IV deficiency in muscle, liver or fibroblasts
Brain MRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (basal ganglia, brainstem, lactate peak)
Liver function tests and coagulation studies during crises
Plasma amino acids, urine organic acids and acylcarnitines to exclude mimics
Ammonia and glucose monitoring during acute illness
redFlags: Intercurrent infection or fasting heralding an acute crisis
reference.prognosis: Outcome is poor: recurrent acidotic crises are frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood, and survivors typically have significant neurodevelopmental disability.
pitfalls: Underestimating crisis risk during apparently minor infections.
Delaying anti-catabolic (glucose-containing) support and correction of acidosis while awaiting confirmatory results.
Attributing chronic lactate elevation to a sampling artefact and missing the diagnosis.
Assuming that stability between crises indicates low risk.
Failing to provide families with a written emergency and sick-day plan.
